'''''Sambucus nigra''''' is a temperate species of tree or shrub in the family [[Viburnaceae]] native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East.<ref name="POWO" /> Common names include '''elder''', '''elderberry''', '''black elder''', '''European elder''', ''' European elderberry''', and '''European black elderberry'''.<ref>{{ITIS |id= 35324 |taxon= ''Sambucus nigra''}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=SANI4|title=Plants profile for ''Sambucus nigra'' L. (black elderberry)|publisher=Natural Resources Conservation Service, US Department of Agriculture|date=2023|access-date=13 June 2023}}</ref> It grows in a variety of conditions including both wet and dry fertile soils, primarily in sunny locations. The plant is widely grown as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] shrub or small tree.

Both the flowers and the berries have a long tradition of culinary use, primarily for [[Elderflower cordial|cordial]] and wine.<ref name= RHSAZ/> Although the plant is commonly used in [[dietary supplement]]s and [[traditional medicine]], there is no [[evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] that it provides any health effect.

==Description==
Elderberry is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{convert|6|m|ft|0}} tall and wide,<ref name= RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Michael and Vikram |isbn= 978-1405332965}}</ref> rarely reaching {{cvt|10|m|ft|0}} tall. The bark, light gray when young, changes to a coarse gray outer bark with lengthwise furrowing, [[lenticel]]s prominent.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968 ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles Second Edition'' Cambridge.{{ISBN| 0-521-04656-4}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are arranged in opposite pairs, {{Convert|10–30|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} long, pinnate with five to seven (rarely nine) leaflets, the leaflets {{convert|5–12|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{Convert|3–5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, with a serrated margin. The young stems are hollow.<ref>Vedel, H. and Lange, J. 1971. ''Trees and Bushes in Wood and Hedgerow''. p. 196. Methuen and Co. Ltd. {{ISBN|0416-61780-8}}</ref>

The [[Plant reproductive morphology#Variations|hermaphroditic]] [[flower]]s have five stamens,<ref name= "Parnell 12">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> which are borne in large, flat [[corymb]]s 10–25 cm in diameter in late spring to mid-summer. The individual flowers are ivory white, {{convert|5–6|mm|frac=32}} in diameter, with five petals, and are pollinated by flies.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

The [[fruit]] is a glossy, dark purple to black [[berry (botany)|berry]] 3–5 mm diameter, produced in drooping clusters in late autumn.<ref name=RHSAZ /> The dark color of elderberry fruit results from its rich [[polyphenol|phenolic]] content, particularly from [[anthocyanin]]s.<ref name="drugs">{{cite web |date=9 December 2025 |title=Elderberry |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/elderberry.html |access-date=6 June 2026 |publisher=Drugs.com}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==

===Subspecies===
{{See also|Sambucus}}

There are several other closely related species, native to Asia and North America, which are similar, and sometimes treated as [[subspecies]] of ''Sambucus nigra'', including [[Sambucus canadensis|''S. nigra'' subsp. ''canadensis'']]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=7320 |title=Sambucus mexicana |publisher=Calflora |access-date=2012-07-16}}</ref> and [[Sambucus cerulea|''S. nigra'' subsp. ''cerulea'']].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=10348 |title=Sambucus nigra ssp. caerulea |publisher=Calflora |access-date=2012-07-16}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
The Latin [[specific epithet]] ''nigra'' means "black", and refers to the deeply dark colour of the berries.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref> The English term for the tree is not believed to come from the word "old", but from the [[Middle English|Anglo Saxon]] {{Lang|enm|æld}}, meaning fire, because the hollow stems of the branches were used as [[bellows]] to blow air into a fire.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elder (Sambucus nigra) - British trees - |url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/trees-woods-and-wildlife/british-trees/native-trees/elder/ |access-date=3 November 2017 |publisher=Woodland Trust |language=en}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==

''Sambucus nigra'' is native to Europe as far east as Turkey.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Sambucus nigra'' L. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=10 February 2022 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30122169-2 }}</ref> It is native in, and common throughout, the [[British Isles]].<ref name="BRC">{{cite web |title=''Sambucus nigra'' |work=Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |publisher=Biological Records Centre and Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/sambucus-nigra |access-date=10 February 2022 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220211023852/https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/sambucus-nigra |archivedate=2022-02-11}}</ref> It has been introduced to parts of most other continents of the world.<ref name="POWO" />

''S. nigra'' grows in a wide range of habitats, including woodland, grassland, hedgerows, scrub, river banks, roadsides, railway banks and waste ground.<ref>{{cite web |last=Bilz |first=M. |date=2020 |title=''Sambucus nigra'' |website=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |publisher=IUCN |page=e.T61684A88328586 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2020-1.RLTS.T61684A88328586.en |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/61684/88328586 |access-date=6 June 2026}}</ref> It is generally associated with open or disturbed, nutrient-rich sites, such as woodland edges, forest gaps, abandoned fields and urban areas; it is not tolerant of drought and avoids saline soils.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Enescu |first1=C. M. |last2=Houston Durrant |first2=T. |last3=Caudullo |first3=G. |year=2016 |chapter=''Sambucus nigra'' in Europe: distribution, habitat, usage and threats |title=European Atlas of Forest Tree Species |editor1-last=San-Miguel-Ayanz |editor1-first=J. |editor2-last=de Rigo |editor2-first=D. |editor3-last=Caudullo |editor3-first=G. |editor4-last=Houston Durrant |editor4-first=T. |editor5-last=Mauri |editor5-first=A. |publisher=Publications Office of the European Union |location=Luxembourg |pages=e013c0f+ |chapter-url=https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/media/atlas/Sambucus_nigra.pdf |access-date=6 June 2026}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
{{multiple image
|direction=vertical
|perrow=2
|image1=Hyphodontia sambuci Eglinton.JPG
|caption1=[[Elder whitewash fungus]]
|image2=Auricularia auricula-judae Eglinton.JPG

Like other elderberries, ''S. nigra'' is subject to [[elder whitewash fungus]] and [[Auricularia auricula-judae|jelly ear fungus]]. Strong-scented flowers in wild populations of ''S. nigra'' attract numerous, minute flower [[thrips]] which may contribute to the transfer of pollen between inflorescences.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scott-Brown |first1=A.S. |last2=Arnold |first2=S.E.J. |last3=Kite |first3=G.C. |last4=Farrell |first4=I. |last5=Farman |first5=D.I. |last6=Collins |first6=D.W. |last7=Stevenson |first7=P.C. |title=Mechanisms in mutualisms: A chemically mediated thrips pollination strategy in common elder |journal=Planta |date=2019 |volume=250 |issue=1 |pages=367–379 |doi=10.1007/s00425-019-03176-5|pmid=31069523 |s2cid=253886497 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Plant.250..367S |url=http://gala.gre.ac.uk/id/eprint/23721/3/23721%20ARNOLD%20Planta%20Sambucus%20and%20Thrips%20AAM%202019.pdf }}</ref>

=== Wildlife value ===
Elder rates as fair to good forage for animals such as [[mule deer]], [[elk]], [[sheep]], and small birds. The fruit are an important food for many fruit-eating birds, notably [[blackcap]]s. Ripe elderberries are a food for migrating [[band-tailed pigeon]]s in northern California, which may sometimes strip an entire bush in a short time.{{cn|date=June 2026}} 

Except for the flowers and ripe berries (but including the ripe seeds), all parts of the plant are poisonous to mammals, containing the [[cyanogenic glycoside]] [[sambunigrin]] (C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>17</sub>NO<sub>6</sub>, [[CAS registry number|CAS number]] 99–19–4).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Campa |first1=Cristiana |last2=Schmitt-Kopplin |first2=P |last3=Cataldi |first3=T R |last4=Bufo |first4=S A |last5=Freitag |first5=D |last6=Kettrup |first6=A |name-list-style=vanc |year=2000 |title=Analysis of cyanogenic glycosides by micellar capillary electrophoresis |journal=[[Journal of Chromatography B]] |volume=739 |issue=1 |pages=95–100 |doi=10.1016/S0378-4347(99)00375-8 |pmid=10744317}}</ref> The bark contains [[calcium oxalate]] crystals.{{Citation needed|date=September 2023}}

==Cultivation==
{{more references|section|date=June 2026}}
''S. nigra'' is grown as an ornamental shrub or small tree, especially in informal hedges, wildlife gardens and mixed borders. The species is also cultivated commercially for flowers and fruit.<ref name="Vojtech2015">{{cite book |last1=Vojtěch |first1=Holubec |last2=Tamara |first2=Smekalova |last3=František |first3=Paprštein |last4=Lenka |first4=Štočková |last5=Vojtěch |first5=Řezníček |title=Crop Wild Relatives and Climate Change |date=2015 |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |isbn=1118854373 |page=310 |chapter=Potential of Minor Fruit Crop Wild Relatives (CWR) as New Crops in Breeding for Market Diversification}}</ref> It is vigorous and adaptable, growing in sun or partial shade although it performs poorly in deep shade or dry conditions.<ref>{{cite web |title=How to grow Sambucus |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/sambucus/growing-guide |access-date=6 June 2026|date=2026}}</ref> It tolerates both wet and dry soils from sand to clay, but grows best on well-drained, organic-rich, slightly acidic soils, about pH 6.0–6.5.{{cn|date=July 2026}} Plants for commercial plantations are usually propagated from own-rooted hardwood cuttings taken from one-year-old shoots. Propagation from seed is less common because seedlings are variable and the seeds have dormancy requirements. Weed control is important during establishment, as black elder competes poorly with other plants.

Some selections and cultivars have [[variegated]] or coloured leaves and other distinctive qualities, and are grown as [[ornamental plant]]s. ''S. nigra'' f. ''porphyrophylla'' has dark maroon or black leaves, and pale pink flowers.{{cn|date=July 2026}} Leaf colour in purple- or golden-leaved cultivars is usually strongest in full sun.
Garden plants need little pruning, but established plants can be hard pruned in late winter or early spring to restrict size or encourage fresh ornamental foliage. In commercial orchards, dormant pruning is usually begun from the second year, removing dead, damaged or diseased wood and stems older than three years, as productivity declines on four-year-old branches. Annual [[coppicing]] to ground level is generally not recommended since most commercial cultivars do not fruit on first-year canes.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 95 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 21 October 2018}}</ref>  
*''S. nigra'' f. ''laciniata'' (cut-leaved elder)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/50846/Sambucus-nigra-f-laciniata/Details |title=''Sambucus nigra'' f. ''laciniata'' / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |access-date=2021-03-06}}</ref>
*''S. nigra'' f. ''porphyrophylla'' 'Eva'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/197771/i-Sambucus-nigra-i-f-i-porphyrophylla-i-Eva-sup-(PBR)-sup/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Sambucus nigra'' 'Eva' | access-date = 21 October 2018}}</ref> ('Black Lace')<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/194381/sambucus-black-lace/details | title = "Sambucus" 'Black Lace' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 2 June 2024}}</ref> 
*''S. nigra'' f. ''porphyrophylla'' 'Gerda'<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/139890/Sambucus-nigra-f-porphyrophylla-Gerda-(PBR)/Details |title=''Sambucus'' nigra f. ''porphyrophylla'' 'Gerda'|publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |access-date=2021-03-06}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
Components of the elderberry plant, including its fruit, contain diverse [[phytochemical]]s, such as [[alkaloid]]s, [[lectin]]s, and cyanogenic glycosides, which may be toxic if consumed raw.<ref name="drugs" />  The seeds and all green parts of the plant contain cyanogenic glycosides.<ref name="nccih">{{cite web |date=1 November 2024 |title=European elder |url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/elderberry |access-date=6 June 2026 |publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, US National Institutes of Health}}</ref> Consumption of berries, leaves, bark or stems, if not properly prepared, may cause [[nausea]], vomiting, and severe [[diarrhea]].<ref name="drugs" /><ref name=nccih/><ref name="msk">{{cite web |date=2020 |title=Elderberry |url=https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/elderberry-01 |access-date=11 July 2020 |publisher=Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center}}</ref> Elderberry plant constituents or products should not be consumed during pregnancy or by people with [[allergy|allergies]] or [[gastrointestinal disease]]s.<ref name="drugs" /><ref name=msk/> Elderberry products may cause [[adverse effect]]s when used with [[prescription drug]]s.<ref name="drugs" /><ref name=msk/>

==Uses==

The dark blue or purple berries are mildly poisonous in their raw state, but are edible after cooking.<ref name="nccih" /><ref name="Fagan-2019" /> They can be used to make [[Fruit preserves|jam]], jelly,<ref name="Fagan-2019">{{Cite book|last=Fagan|first=Damian|title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert|publisher=[[FalconGuides]]|year=2019|isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2|location=Guilford, CT|pages=16|oclc=1073035766}}</ref> [[chutney]], and Pontack sauce. In Scandinavia and Germany, soup made from the elderberry (e.g. the German ''Fliederbeersuppe'') is a traditional meal.<ref name="jorg">{{cite journal | last1=Jørgensen | first1=Ulla | last2=Hansen | first2=Merete | last3=Christensen | first3=Lars P. | last4=Jensen | first4=Karina | last5=Kaack | first5=Karl | title=Olfactory and Quantitative Analysis of Aroma Compounds in Elder Flower (''Sambucus nigra'' L.) Drink Processed from Five Cultivars | journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry | volume=48 | issue=6 | date=2000-05-12 | issn=0021-8561 | doi=10.1021/jf000005f | pages=2376–2383| pmid=10888553 | bibcode=2000JAFC...48.2376J }}</ref>

Commonly, the flowerheads are used in [[infusion]]s, giving a drink in Northern Europe and the [[Balkans]]. These drinks are sold commercially as [[elderflower cordial]] or [[elderflower pressé]].<ref>Kikbracken, J. 1995. ''Easy way guide Trees''. Larousse.</ref> In [[Europe]], the flowers are made into a [[syrup]] or [[Squash (drink)|cordial]] (in Romanian: [[socată]], in Swedish: fläder(blom)saft, in Danish: hyldeblomstsaft / hyldedrik), which is diluted with water before drinking. The popularity of this traditional drink recently has encouraged some commercial [[soft drink]] producers to introduce elderflower-flavoured drinks ([[Fanta]] Shokata, Freaky Fläder). The flowers also may be dipped into a light batter and then fried to make elderflower fritters.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Food for free |date=2012 |publisher=Collins |isbn=978-0-00-743847-1 |edition= |location=London |pages=83 |oclc=761378530}}</ref>

The berries may be made into [[elderberry wine]].<ref name="Fagan-2019" /> In [[Hungary]], an elderberry [[brandy]] is made that requires 50 kilograms of fruit to produce 1 [[litre]] of brandy. In south-western [[Sweden]], it is traditional to make a [[snaps]] liqueur flavoured with elderflower. Elderflowers are used in liqueurs such as [[St-Germain (liqueur)|St-Germain]], and in a mildly alcoholic sparkling elderflower 'champagne', although a more alcoholic home-made version can be made.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

=== Traditional medicine ===
This plant is used in traditional medicine by native peoples and [[herbal medicine|herbalists]].<ref name=drugs/><ref name=nccih/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sambucus+nigra|title=''Sambucus nigra'': Elderberry - European Elder, Black elderberry, American black elderberry, Blue elderberry|publisher=Plants for a Future|access-date=13 October 2017}}</ref> Extracts of the flowers and fruits are used for cold and flu symptoms,<ref name=drugs/><ref name=nccih/> and preliminary clinical research suggests it may have some value in relieving such symptoms.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=nccih/> A 2019 meta-analysis concluded that "supplementation with elderberry was found to substantially reduce upper respiratory symptoms."<ref name="Hawkins2019">{{cite journal |last1=Hawkins |first1=Jessie |last2=Baker |first2=Colby |last3=Cherry |first3=Lindsey |last4=Dunne |first4=Elizabeth |title=Black elderberry (Sambucus nigra) supplementation effectively treats upper respiratory symptoms: A meta-analysis of randomized, controlled clinical trials |journal=Complementary Therapies in Medicine |date=February 2019 |volume=42 |pages=361–365 |doi=10.1016/j.ctim.2018.12.004}}</ref> However, the available research is limited, and there is currently insufficient high-quality clinical evidence to establish its efficacy or safety for the treatment of any disease.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=nccih/>

===FDA warning letters===
Between 2021 and 2023, the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] issued 18 [[FDA warning letter|warning letters]] to American supplement companies falsely advertising elderberry products intended to treat diseases.<ref name="fda-warn">{{cite web |title=FDA warning letters (search "elderberry" by years) |url=https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-actions-and-activities/warning-letters |publisher=Inspections, Compliance, Enforcement, and Criminal Investigations, US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=11 September 2026 |date=2026}}</ref> The main category of the warnings was for the marketing of "unapproved new and misbranded drugs".<ref name=fda-warn/> 

A typical warning letter stated that the "products are not generally recognized as safe and effective for the above referenced uses and, therefore, the products are “new drugs”... which "may not be legally introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce without prior approval from FDA", and that a new drug is approved "on the basis of scientific data and information demonstrating that the drug is safe and effective".<ref>{{cite web |title=Warning letter: EarthLab, Inc., dba Wise Woman Herbals |url=https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/earthlab-inc-dba-wise-woman-herbals-634872-04272023|publisher=Inspections, Compliance, Enforcement, and Criminal Investigations, US Food and Drug Administration |access-date=11 September 2026 |date=27 April 2023}}</ref>
